title: Why the ECB raised rates before headline inflation reached 2%
summary: The ECB raised its three rates by a quarter of a percentage point because waiting for clearer evidence of underlying inflation risked forcing a larger move later. At the 3 February press conference Willem Duisenberg described a consensus on acting immediately. The direction was accepted, while the size and timing had been discussed. There was no formal vote. He declined to turn the size of the rise into guidance about the next meeting. A journalist characterised the introductory assessment as hawkish and another questioned whether markets had been prepared. Those were questions put to the President, not measures of market expectations.

The change had two implementation dates. The fixed rate on the main refinancing operation would rise to 3.25%, starting with the operation settling on 9 February. The marginal lending and deposit rates would rise to 4.25% and 2.25% respectively on 4 February, leaving the distance between the two standing facilities unchanged. The press conference explained the associated decisions. Its discussion of future rates had a different information content from the earlier announcement of the new settings.

The reason to move was the interaction of liquidity, import costs and recovering demand. Private-sector credit had grown 10.5% in the year to December 1999. M3 growth had exceeded its 4.5% reference value throughout 1999. The three-month average of annual M3 growth edged up to 6.1% in October–December from 6.0% in the three months ending in November. The ECB attributed much of that small increase to base effects. Duisenberg also expected base effects to reduce forthcoming growth readings, making them difficult to interpret. A lower reading could therefore emerge even if the economic case for tighter policy remained. Waiting to see whether the November rise had slowed M3 risked treating a statistical change as evidence of transmission (introductory statement and first question).

Headline HICP inflation had risen from 1.5% in November to 1.7% in December 1999, almost entirely because of energy. What changed the medium-term assessment was that commodity and producer-price increases, including non-energy inputs, had been larger and lasted longer than expected, while the economic recovery was broadening. Strong industrial and consumer confidence, improving employment prospects and falling unemployment suggested stronger domestic spending. Robust US growth and recovery elsewhere in the industrial world, Asia and Latin America added external demand. The ECB expected a strong fourth quarter after growth accelerated from the second to the third. That was a judgement about activity before all the fourth-quarter evidence was in.

The currency compounded the input shock. At the end of January the nominal effective euro was approximately 11.5% below its level in the first quarter of 1999. The size and duration of that trade-weighted depreciation could increase import prices and eventually consumer prices. It was neither a one-month EUR/USD change nor the sole trigger for the rate decision. A reporter asked whether the ECB would still have acted had commodities been priced in euros, citing an import-price figure. Duisenberg declined the counterfactual. He regarded differences in US and euro-area cyclical performance as central to past exchange-rate movements, acknowledged possible political influences and offered no date for an appreciation. He attributed the adjacent US and ECB policy dates to the meeting calendars, while acknowledging contacts between policymakers. He offered no signal to sell the Eurosystem’s inherited dollar reserves.

A plausible way for imported inflation to become persistent was through wage agreements then under negotiation across the eleven economies. If workers expected energy-driven purchasing-power losses to recur, they might seek nominal increases that sustained price pressure after the initial shock faded. The ECB hoped that credible action would reassure negotiators about future price stability as well as caution them about settlements. Duisenberg challenged a reporter’s premise that moderate agreements had already settled the issue across most of the area. Some negotiations were still under way. He expected headline inflation to increase for a few months and then ease, leaving annual average inflation comfortably below 2% in both calendar years. He expressed doubt about an area-wide monthly breach and recognised that some individual countries were already above 2%. A 1.5% forecast mentioned in the final question was attributed to the European Commission. It was not a newly released ECB staff projection.

For rates investors, the most interesting market observations came with two distinct horizons. Before the meeting, ten-year euro-area government yields rose between end-December and end-January to their highest since late 1997. The Council interpreted this as consistent with stronger expectations of a lasting expansion. It did not identify the change in expected real rates separately from inflation or term premia. Looking forward, it argued that acting in time to preserve credibility could reduce risk premia. A rise in the policy rate and an expected compression of a longer-term premium could thus occur together. The release provided neither an announcement-window yield change nor evidence that the ten-year yield had already fallen in response.

Finally, Duisenberg believed previous public statements had prepared markets for action, while admitting that the extended advance signalling before the November move may have lasted too long. Precisely when and by how much to act were decisions for the meeting. This left scope for a difference between expecting an eventual increase and being positioned for one on 3 February. The ECB had given guidance on the considerations behind the move and no promised schedule of follow-on increases. Asked about Greek convergence, Duisenberg deferred the formal assessment and described an expectation that rates would converge around entry. Asked about ECB forecasts, he anticipated publication arrangements later that year, with staff work under way. Neither answer altered that day’s operational decision.

questions.question: How much of the February increase had already been priced, and how much news came from the conference?
questions.detail: Recover time-stamped money-market quotes immediately before the decision, between the announcement and the conference, and after the answers on future rates. Compare expected settlement dates with the two implementation dates. This separates news about the current decision from news about the path and tests the President’s judgement that the market was prepared.

questions.question: Were import-price increases spreading into wages and underlying consumer prices?
questions.detail: Follow the particular wage rounds under negotiation using contemporaneous national agreements, import prices, producer prices and HICP categories. Look for breadth, the lag from imported inputs to domestic prices, and what happens as energy contributions roll out. These observations determine whether a temporary price-level shock could sustain a tighter path.

questions.question: Did monetary growth point to spending pressure once base effects were removed?
questions.detail: Use the ECB’s contemporary M3 components and private-credit counterparts, alongside shorter-horizon growth adjusted for seasonal patterns. The bank expected the annual growth calculation to weaken for mechanical reasons. A slowdown in lending and expenditure would have a different implication for the next decision.

questions.question: What drove the increase in ten-year yields before the meeting?
questions.detail: Compare the expected path of short rates with contemporaneous inflation expectations and the behaviour of different maturities. Account for issuer and liquidity differences. A rise in real growth expectations, a larger inflation risk premium and a change in the likely policy path imply different duration exposures even if the observed ten-year move is identical.
